chapter: Billy Berg's, Granz and Nat Cole
title: Lee and Lester's band playing Strayhorn's "A Train" before Duke
summary: Callender says the band got "Take the A Train" from Billy Strayhorn at Billy Berg's and broadcast it before Ellington knew it.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: And 'See You Later, So Long' is going to be one of them. I've also done an arrangement on 'Lush Life,' which is one of my favorite things of all time. Oh, and speaking of 'Lush Life,' it brings to mind Billy Strayhorn. I told you before that we were friends. And here's something that I know very few people would know: That our band, Lee and Lester's band, played 'A Train' before Duke ever saw it.
Not necessarily, because I know that "A Train" was written in Los Angeles down at Evelyn Jellay's(?) house, right?
That's right. Well, we played it...
On 47th Street. I mean, very few people know that "Take The A Train" was written in Los Angeles and not New York.
And since you and Strays were friends, I'm not surprised... I didn't know it before, but I'm not surprised.
Well, now I'll tell you the story.

We were working at Billy Berg's on La Cienega and Pico, and Strayhorn brought us an arrangement for our little band, two tenors, trumpet and a rhythm section, and we played it before Duke ever even heard about it. We broadcast it, and Billy Berg played the part of the announcer, too... So Lawrence Welk gets credit for saying, "The boys will now play 'Take A Train,'" but that's not where it started. Billy Berg was the first one who said, "The boys will now play 'Take a Train'" with Lee and Lester's band, in the early Forties.
Oh, I wonder if anybody has got an aircheck of that. That would be a collector's item.
It really would be. But that's the facts of the matter.
